items.label: section_header
items.text: HINT

items.label: text
items.text: Warning! Many metals corrode, but it is only the corrosion of iron that is referred to as rusting.

items.label: section_header
items.text: KEYPOINT

items.label: text
items.text: Forming rust from iron is a surprisingly complicated process. The iron loses electrons to form iron(Il) ions, Fe²+, which are then oxidised by the air to iron(Ill) ions, Fe3+. Reactions involving the water produce the actual rust.

items.label: section_header
items.text: RUSTING OF IRON

items.label: text
items.text: Iron rusts in the presence of oxygen and water. Rusting occurs with iron and the most common alloy of iron, mild steel (see below).

items.label: text
items.text: The formula of rust is Fe2O3.xH2O, where x is a variable number. It can be called 'hydrated iron(Ill) oxide'. Rusting can be described as a redox reaction – the iron is oxidised.

items.label: caption
items.text: Figure 14.17 Rusting is accelerated by salty water.

items.label: text
items.text: The most obvious way of preventing rusting is to keep water and oxygen away from the iron. You can do this by painting it, coating it in oil or grease, or covering it in plastic. Coating the iron with a metal below it in the reactivity series (e.g. coating steel with tin for tin cans) is also a barrier method.

items.label: text
items.text: Barrier methods are usually quite cheap ways of preventing rusting. A problem with barrier methods is that once the coating is broken, the iron underneath is exposed to oxygen and water and the iron will rust (even the bits that are not directly exposed to the air/water).

items.label: text
items.text: Galvanised iron is iron that is coated with a layer of zinc. As long as the zinc layer is unscratched, it serves as a barrier to air and water. However, the iron still doesn't rust, even when some of the zinc on the surface is scratched away
